strengths: The paper addresses a practically important NLP evaluation question: how collaboration settings affect the outputs of interactive qualitative coding systems. Evaluating these systems within researchers’ workflows is a worthwhile contribution.

The study covers three distinct computational approaches and two contrasting corpora. Shared initializations within systems provide useful experimental control, while the combination of consistency, cohesion, distinctiveness, and correctness offers a broader assessment than topic coherence alone.

The manual assessment of 1,200 document–theme pairs provides valuable evidence beyond embedding-based metrics. Using two annotators with tie-breaking adjudication and reporting Krippendorff’s alpha of 0.632 makes the assessment’s moderate reliability visible. Prompt templates, selected hyperparameters, and participant feedback also provide useful documentation.
weaknesses: The central comparison does not isolate collaboration modality (Section 4). Synchronous conditions involve three-person teams, whereas asynchronous conditions evaluate individual codebooks without consolidation, despite consolidation being part of the introductory definition. Consequently, group size, access to others’ interpretations, and potentially human effort differ alongside synchrony. Participant reuse, with asynchronous sessions always occurring first, introduces additional familiarity and order effects. The findings should be scoped to the actual group-versus-individual comparison unless a better-controlled collaboration study is added.

The statistical evidence is insufficiently justified. The stated design provides only two synchronous and three asynchronous codebooks per system; consistency therefore has only one synchronous codebook-pair, versus three overlapping asynchronous pairs. Tables 1–2 report numerous unpaired t-tests without specifying their observational units or effective sample sizes. Themes and document comparisons sharing codebooks are not independent experimental replications, and participant reuse adds dependence. Session-level results, appropriate uncertainty estimates, and an explanation of dependence and multiple-comparison handling are needed before the significance claims can be trusted.

The proposed metrics need stronger validation as measures of qualitative-analysis quality. Maximum-similarity alignment permits many-to-one theme matches and can be affected by theme granularity, yet resulting theme counts and size distributions are not reported. High embedding similarity does not necessarily preserve analytically important distinctions such as opposing stances. Selecting the nearest 25% of documents also favors cohesive subsets by construction. Sensitivity analyses and human judgments of theme quality would help establish what improvements in these metrics mean.

The correctness evaluation is incomplete and underspecified (Section 5.3). It covers only COVID data, leaving cross-dataset correctness unsupported. Figure 4 reports F1, but the described document–theme verification procedure does not define precision, recall, or the averaging convention. Uniform sampling across themes also requires clarification about whether the target is average-theme or corpus-level correctness. Appendix E reports 0.7–16.1% unlabeled LLM outputs, without explaining their treatment in the quality metrics. Confidence intervals are needed to assess the claimed differences.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite useful implementation details. Section 4’s total of 15 experiments is unclear in relation to the two-dataset evaluation, and the allocation of 33 participants across runs is missing. The exact S-BERT checkpoint, final codebooks, selected prompt per session, decoding settings, and Climate-specific relational configuration are not adequately documented. Annotation outputs and evaluation code are promised rather than supplied. The interview component also lacks a clear sample size and account of how themes were derived.

Several interpretations exceed the evidence. Climate cohesion improvements for the relational and LLM systems are approximately 0.01 in Table 2, which provides limited support for claims of substantially deeper analysis. Explanations based on corpus complexity remain hypotheses because the two corpora differ along several dimensions simultaneously. Broad conclusions about LLM reliability and computational cost likewise rest on one 3B model and one implementation. These issues, together with the design and inference concerns, prevent a sound Findings recommendation at present; reanalysis, fuller reporting, and narrower claims could support a next-cycle revision.
